cultivar: Assam bush (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) seedlings and Tocklai clones (TV series, S3A3, P126)
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea: withered, rolled whole in orthodox rollers, oxidised to a copper-red leaf and fired, then sorted into leaf grades such as TGFOP and FTGFOP1.
harvest_season: March to November; the second flush (late May to June) gives the best, tippy, malty teas, the first flush (March–April) is lighter and the rains crop plainer.
appearance_dry: Long, well-twisted dark brown to black leaf with a sprinkling of golden tips.
taste_profile: Malty and full: dark honey, dried fig and a hint of cocoa, with a brisk, tannic backbone that softens with milk.

brewing.notes: Boiling or just under, about four minutes. Takes milk very well, but a tippy lot from a named garden is worth trying neat first.

vintage_note: Sold through the Guwahati and Kolkata auctions and by private sale as garden invoices, by flush and grade: FTGFOP1, TGFOP, GFOP, FOP and the broken grades. The second flush of the current year is the prized lot (shops label it 'Assam Second Flush 2025' and so on) and arrives from July; first flush is on sale from April–May. Orthodox Assam keeps 2–3 years sealed but is at its best within about 18 months.
description:
Assam orthodox is the whole-leaf black tea of the Brahmaputra valley in north-east India, the world's largest contiguous tea-growing region and the home of the big-leaved assamica bush. It is the malty, coppery, full-bodied tea that most breakfast blends are trying to imitate, and the gardens along the river make it in a style bolder than almost anything else on the shelf.

The leaf is withered, rolled whole in orthodox rollers, oxidised fully to a copper-red and then fired, before being sorted into leaf grades. Low altitude, heavy rain and summer heat drive the bushes hard, and the second flush in late May and June, when the buds are fat and golden, gives the best orthodox teas of the year; the spring first flush is lighter and the rains crop plainer.

A good second-flush orthodox tastes of malt, dark honey and dried fig with a cocoa edge, a thick body and a brisk, tannic backbone. Brew it with water at or just under the boil for about four minutes; it takes milk very well, but a tippy lot from a named garden deserves to be tried neat first, and it will give a decent second steep.

It is sold by garden, flush and grade, through the Guwahati and Kolkata auctions and by private sale. The grade codes (FTGFOP1, TGFOP, GFOP, FOP, and the broken grades BOP and GBOP) describe leaf size and the amount of golden tip, not quality; a plain TGFOP from a good garden can beat a FTGFOP1 from a poor one. Names worth knowing include Halmari, Mangalam, Doomni, Dikom, Harmutty, Khongea and Mokalbari. Orthodox Assam keeps two or three years sealed but is best within eighteen months.

If you only know Assam from tea bags, a single-estate second flush is the tea that will change your mind.
sources_note: Native name given in Assamese (অসম চাহ); the romanisation 'Oxom sāh' follows Assamese pronunciation and could be checked.
